content: Onions are a term used to describe various plants within the genus Allium. When the term onion is used without qualifiers, it typically refers to Allium cepa, also known as the garden onion, bulb onion, or shallot. Allium cepa is only known in cultivation, but its wild relatives are found in Central Asia. Closely related species include Allium vavilovii, native to Iran, though there is some debate about whether these represent true wild species or feral derivatives of cultivated onions. Onions are among the oldest vegetables known to humanity and are used in a vast array of recipes and preparations across nearly all global cultures. They are available in fresh, frozen, canned, pickled, and dehydrated forms. Onions are typically chopped or sliced and incorporated into cooked dishes, fresh salads, or used as a spicy garnish. They are rarely consumed alone and usually serve as an accompaniment to main dishes. Depending on the variety, onions can range in flavor from sharp, spicy, tangy, and pungent to mild and sweet. Pickled onions are often consumed as snacks and are commonly served as a side dish in fish and chip shops in the United Kingdom. In India, onions are a staple food and a fundamental ingredient in Indian cooking, often forming the base for curries or being made into a paste for main courses or side dishes. Onion tissue is frequently used in science education to demonstrate microscope usage due to its large, easily observable cells, even at low magnifications. Historically, onion bulbs have been used as a food source for millennia. Traces of onion remains have been found in Canaanite Bronze Age settlements alongside fig and date stones, dating back to 5000 BC. Onions are native to South Asia and are widely used in Indian cuisine, though it is unclear if these were cultivated onions. Archaeological and literary evidence, such as the Book of Numbers 11:5, suggests that onion cultivation likely began around 2000 years later in ancient Egypt, alongside leeks and garlic. Workers building the Egyptian pyramids were reportedly fed radishes and onions. Onions were easily propagated, transported, and stored, and the Ancient Egyptians worshipped them, believing their spherical shape and concentric rings symbolized eternal life. Onions were even used in Egyptian burial practices, as evidenced by onion traces found in the eye sockets of Pharaoh Ramesses IV. The strong scent of onions was believed to bring breath back to the dead. In ancient Greece, athletes consumed large quantities of onions, believing they lightened the balance of blood. Roman gladiators were rubbed with onions to firm up their muscles. During the Middle Ages, onions were so important that they were used to pay rent and given as gifts. Physicians prescribed onions to aid bowel movements, improve erections, and relieve headaches, coughs, snakebites, and hair loss. Onions were introduced to North America by Christopher Columbus during his 1492 expedition to Haiti. In the early 1500s, onions were also prescribed to help with infertility in women and even for household pets like dogs and cattle. However, recent evidence has shown that onions are toxic to dogs, cats, and other animals during digestion and should not be given to them in any form. Onions have been associated with various medicinal properties and health benefits. Claims have been made about their effectiveness against conditions such as the common cold, heart disease, diabetes, osteoporosis, and other diseases. Onions contain chemical compounds believed to have anti-inflammatory, anti-cholesterol, anti-cancer, and antioxidant properties, such as quercetin. However, there is no conclusive evidence that increased onion consumption directly leads to health benefits. In some parts of the world, onions are used to heal blisters and boils. A traditional Maltese remedy for sea urchin wounds involves tying half a baked onion to the affected area overnight, with the spikes being drawn into the onion by morning. In the United States, onion extract products are used to treat topical scars, though studies have shown mixed results regarding their effectiveness. Some studies suggest they may act as anti-inflammatory or bacteriostatic agents and improve collagen organization in rabbits. Onions may also benefit women at increased risk for osteoporosis during menopause by inhibiting osteoclasts, which break down bone. When onions are sliced, their cells are broken, releasing enzymes called alliinases that break down amino acid sulfoxides to generate sulfenic acids. These acids are unstable and rearrange into a volatile gas called syn-propanethial-S-oxide. This gas diffuses through the air and reaches the eyes, where it reacts with water to form a diluted solution of sulfuric acid, irritating the nerve endings and causing stinging. Tear glands produce tears to dilute and flush out the irritant. Eye irritation can be minimized by cutting onions under running water, submerging them in water, or chilling/freezing them before cutting. Using a sharp knife reduces cell damage and enzyme release. Additionally, leaving the onion root intact until the end of chopping can limit irritation, as the root contains a higher concentration of enzymes. Heat, such as from a candle or burner, can also neutralize the gas. The amount of sulfenic acids released and the degree of irritation vary among Allium species. In 2008, researchers in New Zealand developed no-tears onions using gene-silencing biotechnology. Onions can be propagated from seeds or sets. Onion sets are produced by sowing seeds densely, resulting in stunted plants that form small bulbs. These bulbs are easy to plant and grow into mature bulbs the following year but are less durable than onions grown directly from seeds. Both methods can produce spring onions or green onions, which are harvested while immature. The term green onion also refers to Allium fistulosum, the Welsh onion, which does not produce dry bulbs. Onion varieties include brown, white, yellow, and red onions. Bulb onions, grown from seeds or sets, range from pungent varieties used for dried soups and onion powder to mild and sweet varieties like Vidalia onions from Georgia or Walla Walla onions from Washington, which can be eaten raw. Multiplier onions are raised from bulbs that produce multiple shoots, each forming a bulb. Tree onions or Egyptian onions produce bulbils in the flower head and are hybrids of Allium cepa. Shallots contain the highest phenolic and antioxidant content among onion varieties, followed by Western Yellow, New York Bold, and Northern Red onions. Milder varieties, such as Vidalia and Peruvian Sweet onions, have lower phenolic and flavonoid content and less cancer-fighting ability. In language, onions symbolize complexity and layers, as seen in expressions like layers of the onion. This metaphor is used to describe peeling back layers of something without reaching a core, emphasizing continuity between layers and the absence of a central essence. Onions are also associated with irritation, as in the phrase really dices my onion. In some Scots dialects, onions are pronounced ingin. In Bermuda, onion is a slang term for a Bermudian, reflecting the island's reputation for producing high-quality onions. The feminist poet Carol Ann Duffy uses the onion as a metaphor for love and relationships in her poem Valentine.
